# MiniMax M3.1 Flash Launches: 3x Faster, 70% Cheaper 

 Sofia LindströmSofia Lindström
 AI & Machine Learning

Sofia Lindström

October 19, 2026

15 min read

China’s MiniMax rolled out an updated version of its flagship speed-tier AI model on Monday, October 19, 2026, telling customers that MiniMax M3.1 Flash delivers what the company calls a “generational leap” in agentic tasks, coding, Computer Use, and cybersecurity. Reuters reported the launch directly from Beijing, in a dispatch syndicated by WHTC, where MiniMax said the update makes online inference nearly three times faster than its predecessor while cutting usage costs by 70%. [...] The 70% cost reduction MiniMax is claiming applies to the jump from its prior generation of models to M3.1 Flash, not necessarily to every competitor’s current pricing. Still, the broader trend is unmistakable: token prices for mid-tier coding and agentic models have been falling across the board throughout 2026, driven partly by Chinese labs undercutting each other and partly by efficiency gains in inference serving. MiniMax’s own roadmap illustrates the churn. Reports indicate that M Plan and Token Plan requests previously routed to its M2.5 and M2.7 models are now being redirected to M3.1 Flash, with the older models scheduled for retirement on November 18, 2026, a one-month runway for customers to migrate their integrations.

results.title: China's MiniMax Says Its New AI Model Cuts Agent Costs by 70%
results.content:
China’s MiniMax is taking aim at the cost of autonomous AI, introducing a new model it says can handle agent tasks faster and more cheaply than its predecessor.

The company launched M3.1 Flash on Monday, claiming the model operates nearly three times faster than its previous version while reducing agent task costs by 70%. MiniMax also revealed that its anonymously tested model, known as “Space Bunny,” had processed more than 200 trillion tokens before the official release.

The launch adds another low-cost contender to the increasingly competitive AI model market. But independent evaluations raise an important question for businesses: whether lower inference costs can offset the additional work needed to verify an agent’s output.
